title: Fit a glass screen protector with its alignment tray: seat the tray square round the phone, press, lift it off empty
instruction: Put the screen protector on the phone with its tray: set the tray down over the phone, press the middle of the glass, then lift the tray off and put it down beside the phone.
context: Screen protectors are the second most common phone accessory after cases: in a 2023 YouGov survey of 1,104 US adults, 46% said they use one. Spigen's Glas.tR EZ Fit comes with the glass already mounted in a rigid tray; in Spigen's words: "Simply place the tray over the phone, press the center and watch the glass adhere in place." Its installation video adds: "Place the tray flat on the screen without tilting." Its support page: "please remove the phone case before proceeding." The tray lines the glass up only if it goes on square: it fits closely round the phone, so it has to come down level and within about 2 mm. Set down further off, its rim lands on the phone's edge: it sits proud and crooked and the glass goes down off true. And the glass sticks only once it is pressed down flat: lift the tray without pressing and the glass comes away with it. Done right, the glass is on true and the empty tray comes off.
setup: A desk in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. Three objects. (1) An Apple iPhone 16 (147.6 x 71.6 x 7.80 mm, 170 g; teal aluminium frame, glass front and back), switched off, no case, screen wiped clean, lying screen up on the bare desk, its long side across the robot: centred 27.0 cm forward and 12.0 cm right of centre, its top end (camera) toward the left arm, rocked slightly on its camera bump. (2) Its Spigen Glas.tR EZ Fit installation tray (sizes estimated), clear moulded plastic (drawn dark grey so it shows), 76.4 x 152.4 mm (164.4 mm over its two flat end handles), 25 g: a 2 mm deck with a 54 x 120 mm press window and a 2 mm rim round its edge, and under the deck a skirt 4.5 mm deep that fits round the phone with 0.4 mm to spare a side, its bottom edge chamfered 1.5 mm as a lead-in; seated, the rim stands 5.5 mm above the screen, so the outside of each long wall is 10 mm tall. It lies skirt down on the desk 12.5 cm nearer the robot than the phone, in line with it, its back film already peeled. (3) The tempered-glass protector, 68 x 144 x 0.4 mm with its films, 8 g (drawn blue-tinted so it shows), held adhesive side down in the tray's recess under the window by the tray's strip sticker; with the tray sitting on the phone it hangs 1 mm above the screen.
scoring: Judged at the end; measure with a ruler or calliper and a photo. The glass is on when it is stuck flat on the screen. On a real phone: in a photo taken from above, with the screen off and a lamp reflected in it at a low angle, no air gap (a bright white, silvery or rainbow patch or band, where the glass is not stuck) touches any edge or corner of the glass; small bubbles wholly inside its edges do not count. In the simulation: no corner more than 0.3 mm above the screen (glass held flat there for 0.5 s sticks down flat). Its offset is the most any of its four corners lies from where it belongs (the border between the glass's edge and the phone's edge equal on opposite sides). 1.0: glass on, every corner within 1.5 mm, the tray off the phone (no part of it within 10 mm of the phone below 20 mm up), the hands at least 3 cm from the tray and the phone, everything still for 1 s. 0.5: glass on within 1.5 mm with the tray still on the phone, or glass on within 2 mm with the tray off. 0.25: glass on within 2 mm, tray still on. 0: anything else (glass still in the tray, lifted, tilted, or more than 2 mm off), or the phone pushed more than 30 mm from where it lay or turned over.
reset_notes: Each trial uses up one pre-loaded tray: peel the glass off the screen and wipe the screen, then lay out a fresh tray (the kit has two; Spigen sells EZ Fit refill packs) with its back film peeled. Lay the phone and the tray at their taped marks. Real trial: the maker's 30 s wait and sticker removal (its Steps 6-7) are done by the operator, not the robot. The operator pauses the robot as soon as the press has ended (the fingers that pressed have risen off the glass, the tray still seated on the phone), lets 30 s pass from the press, then, keeping the tray down on the phone with a fingertip, pulls the strip sticker off the tray by its tab and resumes the robot, which lifts the tray off. The pause does not count toward the run limit. If the tray leaves the phone before such a pause, the trial runs on without these steps and is scored as it ends. The simulation needs neither: its strip lets go by itself once the glass has stuck.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; glass, adhesive and films are one 0.4 mm plate. The strip sticker holding the glass in the tray is a 0.1 N lift at each end with a 1.5 mm stretch limit. Adhesion is a rule: flat on the screen for 0.5 s, the glass stays where it lies and the strip lets go, so the robot skips Spigen's 30 s wait and sticker step (in a real trial the operator does both in a pause). Starts after the back-film peel. Tray sizes (rim height from Spigen's video, the rest guessed) and masses are estimates.
